title: Malaria basics, Sri Lanka's road to malaria-free status, and malaria incidence 2000–2024

sources.publisher: World Health Organization, Country Office for Sri Lanka
sources.title: Driven to End Malaria: Ten years of success for Sri Lanka (2026-04-24)
World Development Indicators: Incidence of malaria (per 1,000 population at risk) (SH.MLR.INCD.P3)

facts.text: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites and spreads to people mainly through the bites of some infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.
In 2024 there were about 282 million malaria cases and about 610,000 malaria deaths worldwide.
About 95% of malaria cases and deaths in 2024 occurred in the WHO African Region.
Children under 5 account for about three-quarters of malaria deaths in the WHO African Region.
Insecticide-treated nets and indoor spraying with insecticides are the two core ways of controlling the mosquitoes.

WHO certifies a country as malaria-free when it proves that local transmission has been interrupted nationwide for at least 3 consecutive years and that a working surveillance and response system is in place.
Sri Lanka set up its Anti-Malaria Campaign in 1911.
Malaria outbreaks in Sri Lanka in 1934 and 1935 affected about 1.5 million people and caused nearly 80,000 deaths.
DDT was introduced in Sri Lanka in 1946, and a national malaria elimination programme began in 1958.
Malaria was nearly eliminated in Sri Lanka in the early 1960s but resurged between 1967 and 1969.
Sri Lanka's last reported case of locally transmitted malaria was in 2012, and WHO certified the country malaria-free in 2016.
Since certification, cases brought in from abroad can restart local transmission because mosquitoes able to carry malaria are still present across Sri Lanka.
WHO lists declining clinical familiarity with malaria among the threats Sri Lanka now faces.
To prevent malaria from returning, Sri Lanka has strengthened case detection and mosquito monitoring, follows up imported cases closely, and gives preventive medicine to travellers to malaria areas.
The World Bank indicator counts new malaria cases in a year per 1,000 people at risk.
Derived from the dataset: South Asia fell from 21.6 to 1.5 cases per 1,000 at risk (2000–2024), less than one-tenth; the world rate rose from 58.7 (2016) to 64.0 (2024), above its 2012 level of 62.7.
